title: Thermal Stability and Phase Evolution in the Phosphorus-Containing High-Entropy Alloy Fe<sub>22</sub>Ni<sub>16</sub>Co<sub>19</sub>Mn<sub>12</sub>Cr<sub>16</sub>P<sub>15</sub>.

recollection.starting_material: An as-cast high-entropy alloy with nominal composition Fe22Ni16Co19Mn12Cr16P15 (at %).
recollection.intervention: Thermal annealing/aging at a series of temperatures (≈600 – 1000 °C) for various holding times to study phase evolution and stability, combined with X-ray diffraction, DSC, and electron microscopy.
recollection.structure: Initially a single-phase face-centered-cubic (fcc) solid solution that, upon heating, decomposes into an fcc matrix plus P-rich intermetallic/phosphide precipitates (likely M3P-type) and perhaps some body-centered-cubic (bcc) secondary phase at the highest temperatures.
recollection.mechanism: Phosphorus lowers the solid-solution stability; on annealing it segregates and nucleates nanoscale phosphide precipitates, which pin grain boundaries and retard coarsening, thereby improving thermal stability. Concurrent ordering or formation of a minor bcc phase may occur through diffusion-controlled partitioning of Fe/Cr.
recollection.results: The alloy retains a fine grain size (<2 µm) after 100 h at 800 °C, showing hardness around 450 HV and tensile strength above 1.2 GPa while keeping moderate ductility (~10 %). Differential-scanning calorimetry indicates an onset of phase separation near 650 °C, and volume fraction of precipitates reaches ≈15 % after 24 h at 900 °C.

score.note: The recollection invents a 600–1000 °C annealing/aging study, whereas the key intervention was compositional modification followed by comparison of arc solidification and rapid melt spinning. It incorrectly describes the initial material as single-phase fcc rather than an eutectic/phosphide-containing ingot, with the melt-spun ribbon fully amorphous. The only partial mechanistic overlap is P-driven segregation and phosphide formation via elemental partitioning; grain-boundary pinning, improved thermal stability, and bcc formation are unsupported. All reported grain size, hardness, strength, ductility, time, temperature, and precipitate-fraction values are fabricated or inconsistent with the actual thermal events and enthalpies.
